title: Hashing's Origin: An IBM Memo From 1953
explainer: The hash table's core trick — computing an index that jumps straight to data instead of searching for it — traces to internal IBM memos written by Hans Peter Luhn in January 1953, proposing that records be grouped into 'buckets' by a computed key (hashing with chaining) to speed up lookups. One of the most-used data structures in modern software started as a practical engineer's note on making search faster, not as an abstract theoretical result.

title: Why We Call It a 'Tree'
explainer: The word 'tree' for a branching data structure isn't a programming invention: the British mathematician Arthur Cayley coined the term in an 1857 paper, originally to describe branching patterns that show up when repeatedly applying differential operators, and later used the same structures to count the possible arrangements (isomers) of hydrocarbon molecules. The vocabulary of root, parent, child, and leaf used for binary search trees and heaps descends directly from that 19th-century naming choice.
